title: Why not just renounce?
hookLine: Arjuna spots what looks like a loophole: if understanding is better than action, why not skip the action?
carry: karma yoga: no one can stop acting, so offer it

lines: IF WISDOM IS HIGHER, WHY ACT?
WHY NOT QUIT, AND SIT ON A MOUNTAIN?
cards: Arjuna has been listening carefully, and like any sharp student, he's found what looks like a contradiction. Krishna, you keep praising understanding, steady wisdom, a mind free of desire.
You say that's higher than action. So why push me into this terrible action? Your words are mixed.
You're confusing me. Just tell me the one thing that's best. It's a modern question, too.
If peace is the goal, why not quit? Leave the job, the city, the argument, and go sit on a mountain.

teach.b: Krishna says there are two paths in this world, both taught long ago: the path of knowledge, for those given to contemplation, and the path of action, for those given to work. Then he closes the loophole.
Not by avoiding action does anyone get free of action, and not by renouncing alone does anyone reach perfection. In Sanskrit: na hi kashchit kshanam api jatu tishthaty akarmakrit.

teach.h: NO ONE CAN STOP ACTING, EVEN A MOMENT.
teach.b: No one, not even for a moment, can remain without acting. You breathe. You blink.
Your heart beats. Your nature keeps moving you whether you like it or not. So the choice was never action or no action.

teach.h: STILL BODY, BUSY MIND: A PRETENDER.
teach.b: Someone who holds the body still but keeps dwelling in the mind on the things they gave up, the text calls a mithyachara, a pretender, someone whose outward conduct is a lie.
Better, he says, the one who controls the senses with the mind and gets to work, unattached. Then: niyatam kuru karma tvam, karma jyayo hy akarmanah.
Do the work that's yours; action is better than inaction. You couldn't even keep your body alive without acting.
And the verse that opens tomorrow: the world is bound by action, except action done as yajna, as an offering. So act, Krishna says, for that, free from attachment.
The Gita honors renunciation; Hindu tradition has great renouncers. But it won't let running away pass for freedom.
In Krishna's answer, the mountain doesn't save anyone from their own mind. What frees is how one acts. This is karma yoga; many teachers read it as the householder's path, as true as a monk's.

how: Chapter three of the Gita, Karma Yoga, is often taught as the foundation of the householder's spiritual life in Hinduism: work, family and duty done without attachment, as an offering.

o: action, work, the things you do
a fate you can never escape

games.q: what's inside Krishna's answer — tap the pairs.
p: a pretender: still body, busy mind

s: the Gita tells everyone to give up the world
it says no one can stop acting, even for a moment, and that action is better than inaction.
sitting still while dwelling on what you gave up counts as renunciation
the text calls that person a mithyachara, a pretender.
the Gita names two paths, knowledge and action
and then says neither avoiding action nor renouncing alone brings freedom.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you decide the way to be free is to sit perfectly still and stop acting. what does Krishna say?
o: no one can stop acting even a moment. act unattached, as an offering.
then let someone else act for you.
games.why: na hi kashchit kshanam api: no one can remain without acting, even for a moment. still body, busy mind is a pretender. so act, as an offering.

practice: Sit still and try to do absolutely nothing, then notice: you're breathing, your heart is beating, your eyes blink, thoughts arrive. Even sitting still is full of action, so instead of trying to escape it, offer it.
Many Hindus end a puja or a task with the words Krishnarpanam astu, may this be offered to Krishna; if you don't pray, just think, this too, with each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action, work, deed: chapter three is Karma Yoga, the yoga of action. No one can stop acting, even for a moment; freedom isn't escaping action, it's how you act.
